Win ratio and win odds of prioritized endpoints

Source: vignettes/win-ratio.Rmd
win-ratio.Rmd
library(CorOncoEndpoints)

In a generalized pairwise comparison, every patient of the treatment group is compared with every patient of the control group on prioritized outcomes. Here a pair is decided on OS if possible, otherwise on PFS and otherwise on response, and it is a tie if no outcome decides it. With p_win, p_loss and p_tie the proportions of pairs won, lost and tied by the treatment patient, the win ratio (Pocock et al., 2012) is p_win / p_loss and the win odds (Brunner et al., 2021) is (p_win + p_tie / 2) / (p_loss + p_tie / 2). OS and PFS are compared with the scores of Gehan (1965): the patient with the longer observed time wins if the event of the other patient has been observed.

For planning, Yu and Ganju (2022) approximated the variance of the log win ratio by 4 (1 + p_tie) / {3 r (1 - r) (1 - p_tie) N} for N patients allocated in proportions r and 1 - r. Because the overall proportions of several prioritized outcomes are difficult to specify, Barnhart et al. (2025) computed them from the proportions of pairs won and lost on each outcome as if the outcomes were independent. The generator gives the overall proportions under the dependence implied by the design inputs.

Groups and simulated trials

The two groups below differ in PFS (hazard ratio 0.7) and response rate, and survival after progression does not depend on response (pps.hr.resp = 1), so that the distributions of OS, PFS and response in each group do not depend on the correlation between PFS and response. Responses have a time to response and count only if they are observed by the analysis. Trials with 200 patients per group enrolled over 24 months are analyzed at month 30.

make_arms <- function(rho) {
  ctl <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = rho, death.prop = 0.15,
                 os.median = 15, resp.timing = "ttr", resp.tau = 1.5,
                 ttr.median = 2.5)
  trt <- OncoArm(pfs.median = 6 / 0.7, orr = 0.45, resp.cor = rho,
                 death.prop = 0.15, pps.hazard = ctl$gam0, resp.timing = "ttr",
                 resp.tau = 1.5, ttr.median = 2.5)
  list(Control = ctl, Treatment = trt)
}

The proportions of pairs won and lost are computed for each trial:

# wins and losses of treatment patients (rows) against control patients
gehan <- function(t1, e1, t0, e0) {
  list(win = outer(t1, t0, ">") & matrix(e0 == 1, length(t1), length(t0), byrow = TRUE),
       loss = outer(t1, t0, "<") & matrix(e1 == 1, length(t1), length(t0)))
}
win_props <- function(d) {
  x <- d[d$group == "Treatment", ]
  y <- d[d$group == "Control", ]
  os <- gehan(x$os_tte, x$os_event, y$os_tte, y$os_event)
  pf <- gehan(x$pfs_tte, x$pfs_event, y$pfs_tte, y$pfs_event)
  rw <- outer(x$response_obs == 1, y$response_obs == 1, ">")
  rl <- outer(x$response_obs == 1, y$response_obs == 1, "<")
  tie_os <- !(os$win | os$loss)
  tie_pfs <- tie_os & !(pf$win | pf$loss)
  c(p_win = mean(os$win | (tie_os & pf$win) | (tie_pfs & rw)),
    p_loss = mean(os$loss | (tie_os & pf$loss) | (tie_pfs & rl)),
    w_os = mean(os$win), l_os = mean(os$loss), w_pfs = mean(pf$win),
    l_pfs = mean(pf$loss), w_resp = mean(rw), l_resp = mean(rl))
}
mean_props <- function(rho, nsim = 200, seed = 1) {
  d <- rOncoEndpoints(nsim = nsim, n = c(200, 200), arms = make_arms(rho),
                      a.time = c(0, 24), seed = seed)
  cut <- CutoffData(d, cutoff = 30)
  colMeans(t(vapply(split(cut, cut$sim), win_props, numeric(8))))
}
m0 <- mean_props(0)
m6 <- mean_props(0.6)
round(rbind("Corr(PFS, R) = 0" = m0, "Corr(PFS, R) = 0.6" = m6), 4)
#>                     p_win p_loss  w_os   l_os  w_pfs  l_pfs w_resp l_resp
#> Corr(PFS, R) = 0   0.5520  0.394 0.354 0.2711 0.5265 0.3694 0.3151 0.1645
#> Corr(PFS, R) = 0.6 0.5446  0.393 0.354 0.2711 0.5265 0.3694 0.3152 0.1645

Both scenarios use the same seed. PFS and OS are then the same in the two scenarios and only the responses differ, so the proportions won and lost on OS and PFS are the same.

Overall proportions and the power formula

The overall proportions from the jointly generated endpoints are compared with those computed from the proportions won and lost on each outcome as if the outcomes were independent, and both are used in the formula of Yu and Ganju with N = 400 and a one-sided level of 0.025:

power_wr <- function(p_win, p_loss, p_tie, n = 400, r = 0.5, alpha = 0.025) {
  s2 <- 4 * (1 + p_tie) / (3 * r * (1 - r) * (1 - p_tie))
  pnorm(sqrt(n / s2) * log(p_win / p_loss) - qnorm(1 - alpha))
}
summarize <- function(m) {
  w <- m[c("w_os", "w_pfs", "w_resp")]
  l <- m[c("l_os", "l_pfs", "l_resp")]
  t <- 1 - w - l
  carry <- c(1, t[1], t[1] * t[2])
  joint <- c(m[["p_win"]], m[["p_loss"]], 1 - m[["p_win"]] - m[["p_loss"]])
  indep <- c(sum(w * carry), sum(l * carry), prod(t))
  out <- rbind(joint = joint, independence = indep)
  colnames(out) <- c("p_win", "p_loss", "p_tie")
  cbind(out, win_ratio = out[, "p_win"] / out[, "p_loss"],
        win_odds = (out[, "p_win"] + out[, "p_tie"] / 2) /
          (out[, "p_loss"] + out[, "p_tie"] / 2),
        power = power_wr(out[, "p_win"], out[, "p_loss"], out[, "p_tie"]))
}
s0 <- summarize(m0)
s6 <- summarize(m6)
round(s0, 3)
#>              p_win p_loss p_tie win_ratio win_odds power
#> joint        0.552  0.394 0.054     1.401    1.375 0.790
#> independence 0.564  0.416 0.020     1.355    1.347 0.732
round(s6, 3)
#>              p_win p_loss p_tie win_ratio win_odds power
#> joint        0.545  0.393 0.062     1.386    1.357 0.756
#> independence 0.564  0.416 0.020     1.355    1.347 0.732

With Corr(PFS, R) = 0, the joint proportions give a win ratio of 1.40 and a calculated power of 0.79, and the independence assumption gives 1.35 and 0.73. With Corr(PFS, R) = 0.6, the corresponding values are 1.39 and 0.76 for the joint proportions and 1.35 and 0.73 under independence. Response is consulted only for pairs tied on OS and PFS, so its contribution depends on how response is associated with PFS. Here 200 simulated trials per scenario were used; more trials, or the variance of the log win ratio estimated from them, refine the comparison.

References

Barnhart, H., Lokhnygina, Y., Matsouaka, R. et al. (2025). Sample size and power calculations with win measures based on hierarchical endpoints. Statistics in Medicine, 44, e70096. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.70096

Brunner, E., Vandemeulebroecke, M. and Mütze, T. (2021). Win odds: an adaptation of the win ratio to include ties. Statistics in Medicine, 40, 3367-3384. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8967

Gehan, E. A. (1965). A generalized Wilcoxon test for comparing arbitrarily singly-censored samples. Biometrika, 52, 203-223. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/52.1-2.203

Pocock, S. J., Ariti, C. A., Collier, T. J. and Wang, D. (2012). The win ratio: a new approach to the analysis of composite endpoints in clinical trials based on clinical priorities. European Heart Journal, 33, 176-182. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehr352

Yu, R. X. and Ganju, J. (2022). Sample size formula for a win ratio endpoint. Statistics in Medicine, 41, 950-963. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.9297
